summary.text: Let \(C_0=4,C_1=16,C_2=63\), \(C_{n+3}=4C_{n+2}-C_n\), and \(d_n=C_{n+1}^2-C_{n+2}C_n\). Base calculations and the identities \(d_{n+3}=4d_{n+1}+d_n\) and \(C_{n+1}\ge 3C_n>0\) inductively give \(0<d_n\le C_n\), so \(\lceil C_{n+1}^2/C_n\rceil-1=C_{n+2}\); induction therefore identifies the original extremal construction with \(C\), yielding the claimed linear recurrence.

full_proof.text:
Let \((a_n)_{n\ge 0}\) be the sequence given by the original definition. Thus
\[
a_0=4,\qquad a_1=16,
\]
and, for every \(n\ge 0\), \(a_{n+2}\) is the greatest integer \(k\) satisfying
\[
\frac{k}{a_{n+1}}<\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}.
\]
All terms that occur below are positive, as will follow in particular from the identification with the auxiliary sequence constructed below. Since the denominators are positive, the displayed inequality is equivalent to
\[
k<\frac{a_{n+1}^2}{a_n}.
\]
For any real number \(r\), the greatest integer strictly smaller than \(r\) is \(\lceil r\rceil-1\). Consequently the original recursion can be written as
\[
a_{n+2}=\left\lceil\frac{a_{n+1}^2}{a_n}\right\rceil-1.
\tag{1}
\]
For positive integers \(u,v\), one has
\[
\left\lceil\frac uv\right\rceil=\left\lfloor\frac{u+v-1}{v}\right\rfloor,
\]
so (1) is exactly the integer-division recursion
\[
a_{n+2}=\left\lfloor\frac{a_{n+1}^2+a_n-1}{a_n}\right\rfloor-1.
\tag{2}
\]

We will prove that this nonlinear-looking recursion is satisfied by a linear recurrence. Define an integer sequence \((C_n)_{n\ge0}\) by
\[
C_0=4,\qquad C_1=16,\qquad C_2=63,
\]
and
\[
C_{n+3}=4C_{n+2}-C_n\qquad(n\ge0).
\tag{3}
\]
The first few terms are
\[
4,16,63,248,976,3841,\ldots,
\]
as expected for the original-definition variant.

The key is to control the discrepancy between \(C_{n+1}^2\) and \(C_{n+2}C_n\). Put
\[
d_n=C_{n+1}^2-C_{n+2}C_n.
\tag{4}
\]
We first establish three facts:
\[
d_n>0,\qquad d_n\le C_n,\qquad C_n>0
\tag{5}
\]
for every \(n\). These estimates will locate an integer quotient exactly.

First, direct substitution of (3) into (4), followed by expansion, gives
\[
d_{n+3}=4d_{n+1}+d_n.
\tag{6}
\]
Indeed, the three successive instances
\[
C_{n+3}=4C_{n+2}-C_n,
\]
\[
C_{n+4}=4C_{n+3}-C_{n+1},
\]
\[
C_{n+5}=4C_{n+4}-C_{n+2}
\]
may be substituted into
\(d_{n+3}=C_{n+4}^2-C_{n+5}C_{n+3}\); expanding and collecting terms yields
\[
4(C_{n+2}^2-C_{n+3}C_{n+1})+(C_{n+1}^2-C_{n+2}C_n),
\]
which is \(4d_{n+1}+d_n\).

The initial discrepancy values are
\[
d_0=16^2-63\cdot4=4,
\]
\[
d_1=63^2-248\cdot16=1,
\]
and
\[
d_2=248^2-976\cdot63=16.
\]
They are all positive. Formula (6) now proves \(d_n>0\) by strong induction: if \(n=m+3\), then both \(d_{m+1}\) and \(d_m\) are positive by the induction hypothesis, and hence so is
\(d_{m+3}=4d_{m+1}+d_m\).

We next need a simple growth estimate for \(C_n\):
\[
3C_n\le C_{n+1}\quad\hbox{and}\quad C_n>0
\qquad(n\ge0).
\tag{7}
\]
For \(n=0,1,2\), this follows directly from
\[
3\cdot4\le16,\qquad 3\cdot16\le63,\qquad 3\cdot63\le248,
\]
and all four numbers are positive.

Suppose inductively that the assertion is known at all earlier indices, and consider the index \(m+3\). Positivity of \(C_{m+3}\) follows from
\[
C_{m+3}\ge3C_{m+2}>0.
\]
Moreover, by (3),
\[
C_{m+4}=4C_{m+3}-C_{m+1}.
\]
Thus \(C_{m+4}\ge3C_{m+3}\) is equivalent to \(C_{m+3}\ge C_{m+1}\). The latter certainly follows from the already known inequalities
\[
C_{m+3}\ge3C_{m+2},\qquad C_{m+2}\ge3C_{m+1},
\]
together with positivity. This proves (7) for every index.

We can now prove the upper bound in (5), namely
\[
d_n\le C_n.
\tag{8}
\]
It holds initially because
\[
d_0=4\le C_0=4,\qquad d_1=1\le C_1=16,
\qquad d_2=16\le C_2=63.
\]
For the induction step, (6) and the induction hypothesis give
\[
d_{m+3}=4d_{m+1}+d_m
\le4C_{m+1}+C_m.
\tag{9}
\]
On the other hand, (7) gives
\[
C_{m+2}\ge3C_{m+1}
\quad\text{and}\quad
C_{m+1}\ge3C_m.
\]
In particular \(C_m\le C_{m+1}\), and hence
\[
4C_{m+1}+2C_m\le6C_{m+1}\le12C_{m+1}\le4C_{m+2}.
\]
Therefore
\[
4C_{m+1}+C_m\le4C_{m+2}-C_m=C_{m+3},
\]
where the final equality is (3). Combining this with (9) proves
\(d_{m+3}\le C_{m+3}\), completing the induction. We have therefore established all of (5).

We now use these discrepancy bounds to evaluate the quotient in (2). From the definition of \(d_n\),
\[
C_{n+1}^2=C_{n+2}C_n+d_n.
\]
It follows that
\[
C_{n+1}^2+C_n-1=(C_{n+2}+1)C_n+(d_n-1).
\tag{10}
\]
Because \(d_n\) is an integer and \(0<d_n\le C_n\),
\[
0\le d_n-1<C_n.
\tag{11}
\]
Also \(C_n>0\) by (7). Thus (10)–(11) are precisely the Euclidean division of
\(C_{n+1}^2+C_n-1\) by \(C_n\), with quotient \(C_{n+2}+1\) and remainder \(d_n-1\). Consequently
\[
\left\lfloor
\frac{C_{n+1}^2+C_n-1}{C_n}
\right\rfloor=C_{n+2}+1,
\]
and hence
\[
\left\lfloor
\frac{C_{n+1}^2+C_n-1}{C_n}
\right\rfloor-1=C_{n+2}.
\tag{12}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
C_{n+2}=\left\lceil\frac{C_{n+1}^2}{C_n}\right\rceil-1.
\tag{13}
\]
Thus the positive integer sequence \(C_n\) obeys exactly the original extremal recursion.

It remains to identify it with \(a_n\). We use strong induction. The initial values agree:
\[
a_0=C_0=4,
\]
and
\[
a_1=C_1=16.
\]
If \(a_m=C_m\) and \(a_{m+1}=C_{m+1}\), then (2) and (12) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{m+2}
&=\left\lfloor
\frac{a_{m+1}^2+a_m-1}{a_m}
\right\rfloor-1\\
&=\left\lfloor
\frac{C_{m+1}^2+C_m-1}{C_m}
\right\rfloor-1\\
&=C_{m+2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence
\[
a_n=C_n\qquad\text{for all }n\ge0.
\tag{14}
\]
In particular, (3) becomes
\[
a_{n+3}=4a_{n+2}-a_n\qquad(n\ge0).
\tag{15}
\]
Equivalently, with the index shifted,
\[
a_n=4a_{n-1}-a_{n-3}\qquad(n\ge3),
\]
with initial values
\[
a_0=4,\qquad a_1=16,
\qquad a_2=\left\lceil\frac{16^2}{4}\right\rceil-1=63.
\tag{16}
\]
The subtraction in this recurrence is an ordinary nonnegative integer subtraction: indeed, (3), (7), and (14) show that its result is the positive number \(a_n\).

Finally let
\[
A(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}a_nx^n
\]
be the formal generating function. The coefficient of \(x^n\) in
\((1-4x+x^3)A(x)\) is, for \(n\ge3\),
\[
a_n-4a_{n-1}+a_{n-3},
\]
which vanishes by (15). The three remaining coefficients are
\[
[x^0]:a_0=4,
\]
\[
[x^1]:a_1-4a_0=16-16=0,
\]
and
\[
[x^2]:a_2-4a_1=63-64=-1.
\]
Therefore
\[
(1-4x+x^3)A(x)=4-x^2.
\]
Since the polynomial \(1-4x+x^3\) has constant term \(1\), it is invertible as a formal power series. We conclude that
\[
\boxed{A(x)=\frac{4-x^2}{1-4x+x^3}}.
\]
This proves the conjectured generating function for the original-definition sequence.
